title: Nothing Like the Holidays
full_review:
The formula is as familiar as anything conjured up by the ghost of Christmas past. A large clan reunites over the holidays, there's tension among the siblings and with their in-laws, secrets are revealed and old quarrels reignited. But ultimately, reconciliation -- of one sort or another -- is as inevitable as eggnog.

Though director Alfredo De Villa's frequently humorous drama "Nothing Like the Holidays" (Overture) doesn't advance much beyond this hoary outline, an ensemble cast led by Alfred Molina and Elizabeth Pena adds Latin zest to the predictable proceedings, and there's a strong emphasis on family unity and the permanence of marriage.

Bodega owner Edy Rodriguez (Molina) and his wife, Anna (Pena), ethnic Puerto Ricans, are thrilled to be welcoming their children home to Chicago for Christmas, especially wounded Iraq War veteran Jesse (Freddy Rodriguez).

Also joining the festivities -- which will see the family together for the first time in three years -- are Jesse's sister, Roxanna (Vanessa Ferlito), an aspiring Hollywood actress, and his brother, Mauricio (John Leguizamo), an up-and-coming lawyer married to career-focused banker Sarah (Debra Messing).

While Jesse pursues his old flame, Marissa (Melonie Diaz), pleading with her to forgive him for having dumped her in a moment of uncertainty, and Roxanna waits desperately for a call from her agent (she's clearly not the established star her family imagines), Anna frets over Sarah's failure to provide her with grandchildren.

A far greater worry for Anna is Edy's record as a womanizer. Convinced he's resumed his wandering ways -- he keeps excusing himself to take cell phone calls in private -- the matriarch drops a bombshell by quietly announcing, in the midst of a raucous family dinner, that she's divorcing him.

Provoked by the ease with which his unmarried siblings seem to accept this news, after their initial shock, Mauricio launches into an eloquent defense of marriage as difficult but rewarding emotional work.

When Mauricio hits on the stratagem of bringing in their parish priest to counsel his parents, however, stout Father Torres (Manny Sosa) turns out to be gluttonous and ineffectual, more focused on the next helping of free food than on saving Edy and Anna's union. Unable to quiet the mounting storm of family dissent, Father Torres somewhat desperately invites everyone to join him in prayer, only to be told to shut up.

Such a caricature, together with a frivolous debate about whether Mauricio and the Jewish-born Sarah should have their children baptized, are all the more regrettable because of the many indications of Catholic faith featured throughout. Crucifixes adorn several of the rooms, the entire family goes caroling and, despite their differences, Anna and Edy attend midnight Mass together, though it's made clear that this is something Edy hasn't done for many years.

Though its spiritual values are reliable, when it comes to religion and entertainment, "Nothing Like the Holidays" has all the unwelcome variability of a Yuletide grab bag.

The film contains frequent sexual humor, much crude and crass language and a few uses of profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13
